articles.title: The Gassan School: Three Generations of Living Tradition
articles.image_hint: Gassan blade with ayasugi hada, or any blade with visible flowing grain pattern, or generic high-quality sword photo
articles.content:
The Gassan school occupies a unique position in nihonto history. While most schools faded after the Haitōrei Edict of 1876 abolished the warrior caste's right to wear swords, the Gassan lineage adapted, survived, and continues today. Three names from the modern era — Sadakazu, Sadakatsu, and Sadaichi — represent the bridge from the late Edo period to contemporary swordmaking.

Gassan Sadakazu (1836-1918) was the school's bridge to the modern era. Born into a tradition that traced its origins to Dewa Province (modern Yamagata), he relocated the school's center of activity to Osaka, where he became one of the most celebrated smiths of the Meiji era. His work demonstrates a mastery of the ancient ayasugi hada — a flowing, wavelike grain pattern that became the Gassan school's signature — alongside expertise in Soshu-den, Bizen-den, and Yamato-den traditions. He was eventually designated Imperial Household Artist, a rare honor reflecting his stature.

Sadakatsu (1869-1943), Sadakazu's son and successor, continued the school's traditions with remarkable consistency. His blades show technical refinement and the school's characteristic versatility — he could produce work in nearly any classical style. The Meiji and Taisho periods presented existential challenges for swordmaking, and Sadakatsu's ability to find patrons and continue producing fine work helped ensure the craft would survive.

Gassan Sadaichi carried the tradition into the postwar era, when American occupation policies threatened the very existence of nihonto production. The eventual reestablishment of swordmaking under strict NBTHK-licensed conditions owes much to families like the Gassan who maintained the technical knowledge through difficult decades.

Collectors today value Gassan blades for several reasons. The ayasugi hada is visually distinctive and demonstrates serious technical skill — a poorly executed wave pattern looks chaotic, while a master's work flows like silk. The school's documented lineage from Dewa Sanzan mountain ascetic traditions adds layers of cultural significance. And the relative recency of the work means most pieces are in excellent condition with clear provenance.

For newer collectors, a Gassan piece offers an entry point into traditional craftsmanship that doesn't require navigating the murkier waters of medieval attributions. The signatures are clear, the dates are documented, and the work speaks for itself.

articles.title: Hizen Tadayoshi: The School That Shaped Saga Province
articles.image_hint: Hizen blade or any sword with very refined fine grain hada, or tang shot showing yasurime
articles.content:
Few names in nihonto carry the weight of "Hizen Tadayoshi." The first generation Tadayoshi (1572-1632) founded a smithing tradition that would dominate Saga Province for nearly three centuries, producing generation after generation of distinguished smiths under the patronage of the Nabeshima clan.

The Hizen school's hallmarks are unmistakable to trained eyes. The hada — the surface grain of the blade — is so refined and tightly compacted that it earned the poetic name konuka-hada, "rice bran skin." When viewed under proper lighting, the surface appears almost like polished damascene, smooth yet revealing infinite small variations. The hamon is typically a controlled suguha (straight temper line) or chu-suguha with subtle nie and nioi activity.

Hizen Tadayoshi I — also known as Shodai Tadayoshi or Tadayoshi Hashimoto — studied under Umetada Myoju in Kyoto before returning to Hizen to establish his school. His early signature reads Hizen no Kuni Tadayoshi, later changing to Musashi Daijo Fujiwara Tadayoshi after receiving honorary court title in 1624. Blades carrying the Musashi Daijo title from this period are particularly sought after.

Successive generations — Tadahiro (the second generation, signing Omi Daijo Tadahiro), and continuing through Mutsu no Kami Tadayoshi, Omi Daijo Tadayoshi, and others — maintained the school's distinctive aesthetic. The Hizen school's commitment to consistent technique meant that even later generations produced work of remarkably high quality.

Parallel to the main Tadayoshi line, related Hizen smiths produced equally fine work. Masahiro (sometimes called Hizen Masahiro), Yukihiro, and Tadakuni each carved out reputations. The Hizen tradition was a true school, not a single workshop — multiple lineages working in coordinated style.

What makes Hizen blades particularly valuable for collectors is the combination of technical excellence, documented signatures, and aesthetic restraint. The work is not flashy. There are no spectacular hamon patterns or dramatic boshi to make collectors gasp. Instead, the appeal is one of quiet sophistication — the kind of beauty that rewards extended study.

Identification requires care. The Hizen school's success in producing consistent quality also made it a frequent target for forgers. A reliable papered Hizen sword from a reputable source is always preferable to an unpapered example, however attractive the price.

articles.title: What is Juyo Token? Japan's Cultural Treasure Designation
articles.image_hint: high-end blade photo, gallery quality, or origami/papers if available
articles.content:
The term Juyo Token translates roughly as "important sword," but the bureaucratic English understates what this designation actually means in the world of nihonto. A blade that earns Juyo papers from the NBTHK has been judged worthy of preservation for future generations as a cultural treasure.

The shinsa — judging process — for Juyo classification is held only periodically, typically once per year. Submitted blades undergo evaluation by senior NBTHK judges, with strict standards applied to historical significance, artistic merit, condition, and clarity of attribution. A sword submitted for Juyo consideration must already hold Tokubetsu Hozon certification (the previous tier) and must demonstrate qualities that elevate it above the merely excellent.

The categories of consideration include workmanship that displays exceptional technical skill, historical importance, clear association with named smiths of significant reputation, preservation in exceptional condition, and aesthetic distinction. A sword need not satisfy all criteria, but the judges must agree it represents something culturally important.

Approximate numbers help frame the significance. Since the program began in the 1950s, tens of thousands of swords have been submitted. The cumulative number of designated Juyo Token across all sessions is in the few thousands. While that may seem like a substantial population, it represents a tiny fraction of surviving nihonto worldwide. Each Juyo designation comes with the prestige of having passed expert scrutiny at the highest level outside of government cultural property designations.

Above Juyo sits Tokubetsu Juyo Token — "especially important sword." These represent masterworks of the highest calibre, often by named smiths whose work appears in the Meikan and historical records. The number of Tokubetsu Juyo designations is in the low hundreds. Many are held by museums, prominent private collections, or institutions.

For collectors, a Juyo blade represents a significant acquisition. Prices reflect the rarity and prestige — Juyo papered blades command substantial premiums over Tokubetsu Hozon examples by the same smith, often two to four times more depending on condition and historical importance. The investment is also one of stewardship; owning a Juyo blade carries the implicit responsibility of preserving it for the next custodian.

Government designations — Important Cultural Property (Juyo Bunkazai) and National Treasure (Kokuho) — sit above Juyo in the official Japanese cultural hierarchy. These are administered through the Bunkazai protection system rather than the NBTHK, and the standards are correspondingly more selective. Most National Treasure swords are held in museum collections.

Whether you can afford to collect at the Juyo level or simply appreciate seeing them in published references and exhibitions, understanding what the designation means deepens any engagement with nihonto. These are the swords that scholars and collectors have agreed should outlive us all.

articles.title: The Yasukuni Shrine Smiths: Forging Through the Showa Era
articles.image_hint: Yasukuni or gendai-to blade, military mount, or any sword photo from Showa era
articles.content:
Between 1933 and 1945, a small group of swordsmiths working at the Nihonto Tanren Kai forge on the grounds of Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo produced what are now known as Yasukuni-to, or Yasukuni shrine swords. These blades occupy a distinctive position in nihonto history — they are 20th century products of an explicitly political program, yet many were forged using traditional methods to standards comparable with classical work.

The Tanren Kai was established to produce gendai-to (modern swords) for officers and as offerings, in an era when traditional craftsmanship was being mobilized in service of nationalist ideology. The smiths working there were not amateurs. Names like Yasunori Kajiyama, Yasumitsu, Yasutoku, Yasuhiro Miyaguchi, and others were carefully selected for skill and trained in traditional Soshu and Bizen-den methods.

The conditions at Yasukuni differed from typical wartime production. The forge had access to high-quality tamahagane steel, traditional fuel sources, and time to produce blades in the traditional manner rather than the mass-produced shin-gunto that comprised most military swords of the period. The result is that Yasukuni-to are technically among the finest gendai-to produced.

The smiths typically signed their work with their craftsman name preceded by a poetic or geographical phrase. Dates are typically rendered in the imperial reign system (Showa 16, etc.) rather than Western calendar years.

For modern collectors, Yasukuni-to present a particular set of considerations. The technical quality is generally excellent. The provenance is unusually clear given the recent date. And the historical context is impossible to ignore — these were swords forged with explicitly martial intent during a period of catastrophic Japanese imperialism.

The NBTHK accepts Yasukuni-to for shinsa and papers, treating them as legitimate nihonto. Most papered examples are designated as gendai-to and command prices reflecting their technical quality. Some, particularly by named smiths whose later peacetime careers established broader reputations, can be quite valuable.

Collectors interested in this period often pair Yasukuni-to with study of the broader gendai-to revival that continued after the war. Many smiths who began their careers at Yasukuni — or who trained alongside Yasukuni smiths — went on to be Mukansa-rated NBTHK masters in the peace era, having helped preserve the craft through one of its most difficult periods.

Whatever one's reactions to the political context, the swords themselves represent serious craftsmanship and an important chapter in the unbroken history of Japanese swordmaking.

articles.title: Caring for Your Nihonto: Oil, Storage, and Display
articles.image_hint: shirasaya, koshirae display, or any sword in proper storage mount
articles.content:
Owning a Japanese sword brings ongoing responsibility. These objects have survived hundreds of years not by accident but through generations of careful stewardship. Modern collectors are simply the latest in a long line of caretakers, and the basic practices of maintenance haven't changed substantially in centuries.

The fundamental enemy of any steel blade is moisture and the oxidation it causes. Even the highest-quality nihonto will rust given enough atmospheric humidity, body oil contamination, or simple neglect. The traditional defense is choji oil — a clove-scented mineral oil that forms a microscopic protective film on the polished steel.

To oil a blade, you'll need: pure choji oil (available from sword supply specialists), uchiko powder for cleaning, soft tissue paper or specialty washi, and a microfiber cloth. Process: gently remove old oil with tissue paper from base to tip, never the reverse. Apply uchiko powder lightly along the blade by tapping the ball — this absorbs residual oils. Wipe the powder off completely with fresh tissue. Apply a thin film of new choji oil using a clean section of tissue, again moving from base to tip. The visible result should be a faint sheen across the entire blade with no pooled oil.

How often? In dry climates, once or twice per year. In humid climates, every two to three months. Always after handling, since fingerprints leave salt deposits that accelerate corrosion.

Storage matters as much as oiling. Traditional shirasaya — plain wood scabbards of magnolia (honoki) — provide superior protection compared to fancy lacquered koshirae for long-term storage. The wood breathes, regulating moisture, while the simple design prevents the metal fittings of formal mounts from contacting the blade. If you have both shirasaya and koshirae for the same blade, store the blade in the shirasaya and keep the koshirae as a complete display piece.

Display considerations include light, humidity, and security. Direct sunlight will discolor wood scabbards and degrade silk wrappings. Humidity should ideally remain in the 40-50% range — too dry causes wood to crack, too humid invites rust. Climate-controlled rooms work best; if those aren't available, silica gel packets in the storage area help.

Never handle a blade with bare hands. Body oils leave permanent marks that even professional polishing cannot fully erase. White cotton gloves are standard. Never touch the blade itself — handle only the tang, scabbard, or other appropriate areas.

If rust appears, do not attempt to remove it yourself. Mild surface oxidation may be addressable through proper cleaning and re-oiling, but anything resembling pitting requires consultation with a qualified togishi (sword polisher). Amateur attempts at rust removal have permanently damaged countless historical blades.

Most importantly: develop a relationship with a togishi early in your collecting career. Even if your collection is small, knowing whom to call when something goes wrong is invaluable. The community of qualified Japanese sword polishers outside Japan is small but accessible to anyone who asks at NBTHK or NTHK events.

articles.title: Reading a Sword Mei: Signatures, Dates, and Inscriptions
articles.image_hint: close-up of nakago with mei signature visible, tang shot, or any blade with kanji visible
articles.content:
The mei — signature — inscribed on a sword's nakago (tang) is your first window into its identity. Learning to read mei opens up the entire world of nihonto study, even if you don't read Japanese.

Mei placement follows conventions. On a katana mounted edge-up, the signature side is the side facing away from the body when worn. On a tachi (the older sword type, worn edge-down suspended from the belt), the signature side is the side facing outward when worn. This distinction matters: smiths sign on the omote (front) side, and the mei orientation tells you immediately how the sword was intended to be worn.

Smiths typically sign their personal name, often preceded by a province or title. Hizen no Kuni Tadayoshi reads as "Tadayoshi of Hizen Province." Musashi Daijo Fujiwara Tadayoshi adds the courtesy title received from the imperial court (Musashi Daijo) and clan name (Fujiwara). Some smiths sign only a single name; others use elaborate signatures with multiple titles.

Many signatures include a date on the ura (reverse) side. Dates use traditional Japanese era names and sexagenary cycle markers. A date reading Genroku junen rokugatsu kichijitsu translates to "Genroku 10th year, 6th month, auspicious day" — corresponding to a summer day in 1697. Most reference books include era conversion tables.

A nakago itself reveals much beyond the signature. The shape — kuri-jiri (chestnut-bottom), iri-yamagata (mountain-peak), kengyo (pointed), funa-gata (boat-shaped) — varies by school and period. The file pattern (yasurime) on the nakago surface also tells you something: kiri yasurime (horizontal), o-suji-chigai (large diagonal), katte-sagari (right-falling), etc. Particular schools used distinctive yasurime, and matching a tang's filing to the school of the claimed smith is one authentication step.

The patina of the nakago — its color, texture, and overall character — is impossible to fake convincingly. A nakago from 1600 has 425 years of natural oxidation creating a deep, layered patina that reflects light in characteristic ways. New steel hammered to simulate this aging will reveal its origins under careful examination.

What about no signature? Mumei (unsigned) blades are common — many were polished so frequently over the centuries that the nakago was shortened (suriage) and the original signature lost. A mumei blade can still be excellent. Attribution to a smith or school relies on workmanship — the sugata (overall shape), jihada (grain), hamon (temper line), boshi (kissaki temper pattern), and other features.

Beware these signature situations: gimei (false signatures, where a forger added a famous name to a lesser blade) are common with valuable smith names; orikaeshi-mei (folded-over signatures, preserved by reshaping the nakago when shortening); and saka-mei (reversed signatures, where the smith signed on the opposite side for stylistic or historical reasons).

For serious study, invest in two reference works: Hawley's Japanese Swordsmiths is the standard English-language catalog of smiths and signature variants, and Nihonto Koza by Honma Junji discusses signature authentication in depth. Combined with hands-on study at NBTHK exhibitions and sword clubs, they form the foundation of identification skill.

articles.title: The Goto Family and the Art of Sword Fittings
articles.image_hint: tsuba, menuki, kozuka, or any sword fittings - the Goto pieces from gallery if available
articles.content:
While sword blades draw most collector attention, the metal fittings that completed a samurai's daisho — the tsuba (guard), menuki (hilt ornaments), fuchi-gashira (collar and pommel), and kozuka (utility knife handle) — represent an equally refined artistic tradition. Among the families specializing in these fittings, the Goto stand apart for their seventeen-generation continuity from the Muromachi period through the Meiji era.

Goto Yujo (1440-1512), the founding generation, established the family workshop in Kyoto under the patronage of the Ashikaga shogunate. His specialty was carving shakudo — an alloy of copper and gold that develops a distinctive black-purple patina through chemical treatment. The shakudo provided a ground against which gold ornament could be set in dramatic contrast. The Goto style emphasized restrained imagery with extreme technical refinement: dragons, lions (shishi), peonies, and family crests rendered at small scale with jeweler-grade precision.

Each Goto generation maintained the workshop's stylistic continuity while adding personal innovations. Goto Sokujo, the second generation, established many of the conventions later associated with Goto work. Goto Joshin, Mitsutsugu, Tokujo, and others continued through the Edo period. The family eventually split into the Honke (main line) and several Bekke (branch lines), each preserving the Goto aesthetic while developing local variations.

Particular generations are individually celebrated. Goto Ichijo (1791-1876), the seventeenth and final generation, represents the culmination and ending of the tradition. Working into the Meiji period when sword culture was suddenly abolished, Ichijo produced some of the most technically refined and aesthetically sophisticated work of the entire lineage. His pieces are often signed and dated, providing rare clarity for collectors.

The technical methods of Goto work involved: forging the shakudo or shibuichi base; engraving the design in nanako (fish-roe) ground, where countless tiny dots are punched in even rows to create a textured background; carving the figural elements in high relief; and inlaying gold using uttori (foil application) or moriagi (built-up relief) techniques. A single first-rate Goto piece could represent months of master-level work.

For collectors, Goto fittings represent some of the most accessible high-quality nihonto artifacts. A complete Goto-style daisho-soroe (matched pair of fittings for daito and shoto) commands serious prices, but individual pieces — a single menuki, a kozuka with classical theme — can be acquired at price points that bring serious tradition into smaller collections.

Identification of Goto work depends on understanding both the workshop conventions and individual generations. Goto pieces sometimes carry kao (workshop seals) and signatures, but many are unsigned, identified by stylistic and technical features. Reference works specific to the Goto family help organize the body of work.

Beyond their value as individual objects, Goto fittings represent something larger: a documented family lineage maintaining a specific aesthetic tradition across four centuries. That is exceedingly rare in any art form, in any culture, and worth contemplating when handling even a small kozuka.

articles.title: Tachi vs Katana: How Sword-Wearing Changed Japanese History
articles.image_hint: tachi or katana koshirae, sword mount, or any blade with visible curvature showing tachi-vs-katana differences
articles.content:
The terms tachi and katana both translate as "sword," but in nihonto terminology they refer to specific sword types distinguished primarily by how they were worn — and that distinction is far from trivial. The shift from tachi to katana between the late Kamakura and Muromachi periods reflects a fundamental transformation in Japanese warfare and society.

A tachi is a sword worn suspended edge-down from the belt, typically using two cords (obitori) attached to bands on the scabbard. This was the standard sword type from the Heian period through the early Muromachi period, roughly the 9th through 14th centuries. The wearing style reflects mounted combat: a horseback warrior drew the tachi in a single motion that brought the blade down across the enemy with the weight of the horse behind the strike.

The katana, by contrast, is worn edge-up thrust through a belt sash (obi). This style emerged as samurai combat shifted away from horseback engagement toward foot combat in close quarters. Edge-up wearing allowed faster drawing — the famous iaijutsu and iaido draw-and-cut motions are only possible with katana mounts.

Physically, tachi and katana can be similar blades. Many tachi were later remounted as katana when fashion changed; the original blade itself remained the same, but it was now worn differently. This historical reality complicates simple distinctions — an Osafune Kanemitsu blade originally made as a tachi in 1340 might today be classified as a katana because of how its surviving koshirae was constructed during the Edo period.

For collectors and scholars, the distinction is established through several markers. The signature side (omote) of a tachi faces outward when worn edge-down; on a katana, the omote faces outward when worn edge-up. Because a tachi is suspended cutting-edge-down, its signature appears with the characters reading downward toward the kissaki when the sword is held in normal viewing position; a katana signature reads from the nakago end toward the kissaki when held the conventional way.

Length conventions also evolved. Early Heian-period tachi were often quite long, well over 80 centimeters in blade length, suited to mounted cutting at full extension. Edo-period katana converged around 70-75 centimeters as the practical compromise for foot combat in urban environments.

The shift from tachi to katana parallels Japan's transition from the imperial-aristocratic warrior tradition to the more pragmatic, urbanized samurai class of the Sengoku and Edo periods. By the time of the Tokugawa shogunate's establishment in 1603, katana wearing was effectively universal among samurai. Tachi mounts persisted primarily for ceremonial occasions, court appearances, and shrine offerings — preserved as a connection to the older warrior tradition rather than for practical use.

For modern collectors, the distinction affects how a sword is displayed. A tachi belongs on a tachi-kake (suspended display stand), edge-down. A katana belongs on a katana-kake (horizontal rack), edge-up. Confusing the two when displaying nihonto is a common mistake that signals unfamiliarity with the tradition.

Understanding which type of sword you're looking at tells you immediately something about when it was made, how it was carried, and what role it played in the warrior's daily life. Two sword types — one fundamental cultural transition.

articles.title: Why Bizen Province Produced Japan's Finest Blades
articles.image_hint: Bizen-style hamon, choji pattern, Osafune blade if available, or any blade with prominent hamon activity
articles.content:
For roughly five centuries, from the late Heian period through the mid-Muromachi era, Bizen Province — corresponding to modern Okayama Prefecture — was the heart of Japanese swordmaking. More master smiths, more named schools, more documented production, and arguably more surviving masterworks come from Bizen than from any other single region. Understanding why involves geography, geology, economics, and tradition.

The geographic factors begin with iron sand. Bizen Province sits on deposits of high-quality satetsu — iron-rich sand collected from riverbeds and produced by weathering of magnetite-bearing rocks. Bizen satetsu was renowned for its purity and consistency, two qualities essential for producing the homogeneous tamahagane steel that traditional Japanese smelting (tatara) requires.

The forests of Bizen provided the second essential resource: hardwood charcoal. Sword forging consumes enormous quantities of high-quality charcoal — not as a fuel for power but as a precisely-controlled reducing atmosphere during forging and heat treatment. Bizen's hardwoods, particularly the oak and chestnut species suited to slow controlled burning, produced charcoal with the carbon content and burning characteristics smiths preferred.

Geography also placed Bizen at a commercial crossroads. The province sits on the Setouchi coast facing the Inland Sea, with easy water access to Kyoto, Osaka, and the western daimyo domains. Finished blades could move efficiently to markets, and raw materials and skilled artisans could move into the province. This created a positive feedback loop: success attracted talent, talent improved quality, improved quality attracted more buyers, expanded buyer demand justified expanded production.

The result was the emergence of Osafune as a swordmaking center of nearly industrial scale (for its era). Multiple schools coexisted: Ichimonji, Osafune, Hatakeda, Ukai, Yoshioka, and others. Master smiths trained generations of apprentices in workshops that operated continuously across centuries. Names like Mitsutada (founder of the Osafune school in the 1240s), Nagamitsu, Kagemitsu, Kanemitsu, Mitsutsugu, and Mitsuhiro define the high points of medieval Japanese swordmaking.

The Bizen aesthetic centered on the choji hamon — a temper pattern resembling clove flowers, with rounded heads and narrow stems creating a rhythmic, almost musical visual effect along the blade edge. The school's mastery of midareba (irregular hamon) and complex utsuri (the secondary temper effects visible above the main hamon) defined what collectors mean by "Bizen quality."

The decline of Bizen as a center began in 1590, when massive flooding (the Yoshii River disaster of Tensho 18) devastated the Osafune area, destroying workshops, killing many smiths, and disrupting the centuries-old apprenticeship lineages. The school never fully recovered. Bizen smiths continued to work into the Edo period, but the era of dominance had passed.

For modern collectors, Bizen swords represent both opportunity and challenge. The opportunity: an enormous body of surviving work, with named smiths represented across many price points. The challenge: precisely because so much survives, the field includes both genuine masterpieces and many lesser pieces, plus accumulated centuries of attribution debates and disputed signatures.

A papered Bizen sword from a respected dealer, supported by NBTHK or NTHK certification, represents one of the safest and most rewarding entries into serious nihonto collecting. The history these blades carry is the history of Japanese swordmaking itself.
